text: Every script you've written in this course — provisioning, tagging, reconciling, scheduling — is code, and code belongs in a Git repository, not a folder on one person's laptop. If only one machine holds the real copy, the team doesn't actually have that automation; one person does, and only for as long as that laptop keeps working and stays reachable.

Source control earns its place for four concrete reasons: version history keeps every past version of a script around, code review puts a second set of eyes on it before it ever runs against anything real, rollback means reversing a bad change instead of rebuilding from memory, and team visibility means everyone on the team can see what automation actually exists.

Take a real pull request on a cleanup script. The original loop trusted an env=test tag alone to decide what gets deleted. A reviewer reading the diff noticed tagging mistakes happen in practice and asked for a notlike prod-* filter before approving the merge — catching the risk sitting in a diff, days before the script was ever allowed to execute.

Version history also gives you a real rollback, not just a backup you hope exists. git log shows every past version of one file; git revert undoes a specific commit cleanly, without guessing at what the working version used to look like. A script that only ever gets saved over has no equivalent — overwrite it once, and the old working version is simply gone for good.

A shared repository means the whole team can see what automation exists, read exactly what each script does, and check who changed it last and why — instead of automation scattered across individual laptops that nobody else can find, audit, or safely build on top of. Next up: why running that same script from a real pipeline matters just as much as writing it well in the first place.
